AfriScan · Kenya · Wayleaves, reserves and project land

Know what stands inside your wayleave in Kenya

AfriScan maps structures, excavations, tracks and cleared ground along pipelines, transmission and distribution lines, roads, railways and fibre routes, and inside mining and project areas. Each result is measured against your wayleave or reserve width, dated to the image it came from, checked by a person, and delivered as GIS files and a PDF report.

  • 30 m · 40 mWayleaves in published RAPs for 132 kV and 220 kV lines
  • The notice dateThe date full compensation is valued at
  • Every 500 mRanked by the structures it holds

Our published sample is from Mozambique: the route of a high-pressure gas pipeline, with its 100 m band, on a Copernicus Sentinel-2 scene of 2 August 2026. Contains modified Copernicus Sentinel data 2026.

The rules behind the work Land Act 2012 ss.2, 107A, 143–148 · Energy Act 2019 s.170 · Petroleum Act 2019 · Kenya Roads Act s.49 · Mining Act 2016 s.153 · Civil Aviation (UAS) Regulations 2025 · Survey Act s.42 · Data Protection Act 2019 · IFC Performance Standard 5

Dated records for wayleaves and acquisitions

Kenyan land law turns on what stood where, and when

The Land Act 2012 ties a wayleave, its notices and its compensation to the land and to dates. A wayleave holder needs a dated, measured record of what stands in the corridor. That is what we deliver.

Land Act, s.143

The wayleave runs with the land

A wayleave created for national or county government, a public authority or a corporate body attaches to the servient land and binds every owner and occupier from time to time, however they hold or occupy it.

Land Act, s.144(4)

Notice reaches everyone on the route

Before a wayleave is created, the applicant serves notice on all occupiers, including holders of customary pastoral rights, the county, and everyone in actual occupation of urban and peri-urban land along the route.

Land Act, s.148

Survey damage is compensated too

Compensation covers the use of the land and damage to trees, crops and buildings, including damage from the preliminary work that surveyed or fixed the route, paid promptly by the applicant.

Land Act, ss.2 and 107A(9)

Valued at the notice date

“Full” compensation restores the value of the land and its improvements as at the date of the notice of intention to acquire. On compulsory acquisition, occupants in good faith without title are compensated on six years’ occupation and for improvements made before the notice is published in the Gazette.

A “building” in the Act is any structure or erection of any kind, permanent or temporary, movable or not, finished or not (section 2), so kiosks, stalls, mabati sheds and jua kali workshops all count. The wayleave law guide sets out the procedure from notice to Gazette order, with the sections behind each step.

Why it matters now

Corridors are being built and extended

Kenya is adding lines, rails and fibre while older wayleaves fill up. Each new corridor starts with a notice, a census or a cut-off date, and each one later asks what stood there.

Power

A transmission grid still growing

Twenty-nine transmission lines are due for completion by 2028 (KBC, 4 September 2025), with interconnectors to Ethiopia, Tanzania and Uganda and further lines planned under the Transmission Master Plan 2025–2044.

Resettlement

Cut-off dates older than the lines

Published resettlement action plans for lines not yet built fixed their cut-off dates in December 2021, and in one county November 2022. Each provides for re-ratifying the cut-off date by Gazette notice after a delay of two years or more.

Transport and fuel

New rail, new pipelines

Work on the standard gauge railway from Naivasha to Kisumu and Malaba was launched in March 2026 (Capital FM, 21 March 2026). A new eastern pipeline from Mombasa to Nairobi and a cross-border line from Eldoret towards Uganda are planned.

Telecoms

Fibre in the road reserve

About 13,000 km of national backbone fibre is in place (Capital FM, 15 October 2025), and the Digital Superhighway programme aims for 100,000 km (Capital FM, 30 January 2026). Much of it runs in road reserves, where utilities must relocate on the road authority’s written request (Kenya Roads Act, s.27).

What you receive

A dated register your wayleave, land and GIS teams can use

  • Each structure listed with an ID, its distance to the centreline, its band, its chainage and its coordinates.
  • Bands you set: for example 0–15 m and 15–30 m either side for a 30 m wayleave, or the width in your gazette order or RAP.
  • Every 500 m segment rated high, medium or low by the number of structures it holds, with the busiest segments ranked first. It is a count rule, not a safety rating.
  • The image date and source for each feature.
  • Change since the last scan: new and removed structures, flagged automatically and confirmed by a reviewer.
  • GeoPackage, GeoJSON, KMZ and Shapefile layers, an interactive map file that opens in a browser, and a PDF report in English.

Neutral records

Land and assets, never people

We map structures, dates and distances. We do not identify people, and we do not decide whether a structure is authorised: that is for the wayleave holder, the National Land Commission and the courts. Our records are made to support lawful processes, including notices and compensation under the Land Act and lender standards such as IFC Performance Standard 5.

Checked by a person

Building footprint datasets and detection models propose; an analyst reviews each structure before the report is made.

Dated and credited

Each report names its imagery and, where the source provides it, the capture date. Map-service basemaps are never passed off as dated imagery.

Scheduled, never “real‑time”

Satellites capture images on particular dates, so repeat scans follow a schedule agreed with you, with a change notice after each one.

Structures, not personal data

The register carries IDs, coordinates, dates and distances, and no names. Personal data stays in your census. See data protection in Kenya.

Satellite first, drones where they add detail

Two routes to the picture, and the rules for each

Satellite imagery and your own data. A register starts from your route file and dated satellite imagery, open building datasets or the orthophotos you already hold. Most corridors can be screened this way without anyone flying, however long the route and whichever counties it crosses.

Drone detail. Under the Civil Aviation (Unmanned Aircraft Systems) Regulations 2025, commercial drone work needs an RPAS Operator Certificate that KCAA issues only to a company registered in Kenya, with its principal place of business there and a security clearance from the Ministry responsible for defence. So where a stretch needs drone detail, the flights are carried out by such a company, subject to the approvals and security clearances each job requires: KCAA authorisation of the operation, specific permission near high-tension lines, and one month’s written notice to the Director of Surveys under the Survey Act. The proposal names the company that will fly, so your team can check its certificate.

The Kenyan drone-law guide

Who authorises what, the operator certificate and its defence clearance, the 30 m and 400 ft limits, the data rules and a 13-point checklist for anyone commissioning a drone survey, with sources, last reviewed 27 September 2026.

Drone law in Kenya

Where we work

The whole country from satellite, field work where it is safe

Satellite registers cover any corridor in Kenya. Field and drone work does not go where the UK, Canadian, US or Australian government advises against travel (FCDO, updated 4 September 2026; Global Affairs Canada, updated 24 September 2026; US State Department, 17 March 2025; Smartraveller, updated 27 January 2026):

  • Mandera, Wajir and Garissa counties;
  • Lamu County, except Lamu Island and Manda Island;
  • Tana River County;
  • the Kilifi coast north of Malindi;
  • Turkana and Marsabit within 110 km of the South Sudan and Ethiopia borders;
  • West Pokot and western Turkana.

Corridors and project areas there are mapped from satellite imagery only. Elsewhere, any field or drone work is planned around the travel advice current at the time.

What a satellite register needs

  • A route or boundary file, or tower and kilometre-post coordinates
  • The widths to report
  • The dates that matter: a notice, a Gazette order, a cut-off date
  • No site visit, no flight and no landowner letters

How we work · Methodology

For procurement and compliance teams

Tenders, preferences and data

Public bodies in Kenya are moving their procurement onto the e-GP system. The Public Procurement and Asset Disposal Act gives preferences to citizen contractors and requires foreign tenderers in international tenders to source at least 40 per cent of their supplies from citizen contractors. Our notes set out what applies to this kind of work and what to ask any supplier for.

Working with AfriScan in Kenya

Structure registers are designed to carry no personal data: IDs, coordinates, dates and distances. The Data Protection Act 2019 still applies to imagery and to anything a register is combined with, and it reaches processors outside Kenya.

Frequently asked questions

Which widths do you measure?

The width in your gazette order, easement, wayleave agreement or resettlement action plan. KETRACO’s published resettlement action plans, for example, use a 30 m wayleave (15 m each side of the centreline) for a 132 kV line and 40 m (20 m each side) for a 220 kV line. For pipelines, roads and railways, send the width that applies to each section, or the reserve as a polygon, and each structure is reported with its distance to the centreline and the band it falls in.

Can you show which structures were there before the notice or the cut-off date?

Only by comparing dated images. A structure can be dated to the interval between the last image that does not show it and the first image that does, so the record is only as precise as the imagery on either side of the date. Archive coverage varies by place and season, and the proposal says which dated scenes exist for your corridor before you commit.

Do we need a drone survey?

Usually not. Most corridors can be screened from satellite imagery without anyone flying. Where a stretch needs more detail, drone flights are carried out by a company registered and based in Kenya with a current KCAA RPAS Operator Certificate, subject to the approvals and security clearances each job requires, and after one month’s written notice to the Director of Surveys. See drone law in Kenya.

What about cloud in the rainy seasons?

Optical satellite imagery cannot see through cloud, so captures are planned around the rains and each register uses the clearest dated scene for each stretch. Radar comparisons can show larger changes, such as clearing, earthworks and new large buildings, even under rainy-season cloud, and areas they flag are followed up on optical imagery or with a drone check.

Do you work in Mandera, Wajir, Garissa, Lamu, Tana River or West Pokot?

From satellite imagery only. We send no one into the counties and border areas where the UK, Canadian, US or Australian government advises against travel, and no drone flies there. A satellite register needs no one on the ground, so those corridors can still be mapped.

Can you tell us which structures are unauthorised?

No. We map what stands where, how far it is from the line and when it first appears in the imagery. Whether a structure is authorised, predates the wayleave or qualifies for compensation is for the wayleave holder, the National Land Commission and the courts to decide. The register gives them a dated, located list to work from.

Is the register a survey under the Survey Act?

No. Surveys for registrable title documents and boundary surveys are for surveyors under the Survey Act (section 36). Our registers are monitoring and planning records built from imagery. They tell your surveyors, wayleave officers and RAP teams where to look.

Know what stood in the corridor on the date that matters.

Send the route (KML, KMZ, GeoJSON, Shapefile, GPX or GeoPackage), the county or counties it crosses, the wayleave or reserve width from the gazette order, easement or resettlement action plan, and any notice, Gazette or cut-off date the record must reflect. We reply with a scope, an imagery plan and a written proposal.
